utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could the Registrar please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We do without the appearances. They are as usual. I assume Mr. Dokmanovic can hear me well in Serbian. Thank you. First of all, let me thank both parties again for being so cooperative and for submitting the written text of their closing statements. It is greatly appreciated by this court. I understand we are going to hear two witnesses, one for the Prosecution and one for the Defence, but probably before that, we have a few housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honour wants to attend to those matters, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Actually, I was expecting that you would propose -- the matters of which I was thinking were the evidence, the various exhibits which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Fair enough. If that's what Your Honour wishes to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We're in a position to respond to all those matters. I think I might ask Mr. Williamson to address Your Honours on them because he has looked at all of the issues overnight and can indicate what the position is. It's a collective effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday we received from the Defence the translations of all of these materials that came in through Mr. Pavlovic, and so I can go through these one by one. Some of them we have objections to and some we do not, so if perhaps we can just go through those exhibits relatively quickly. As to Defence Exhibit 116, we would object to its admission on the basis of relevance. Do you want me to go through the entire list, or do you want to make rulings as we go through on each item?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us make rulings as you go through each item. So you said 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, which appears to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: -- an inventory of violations of importation of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you feel it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We would object to this on the basis of relevance. And, Your Honour, if I might? The next one involves the same subject matter, so our objection would be the same to it, 117, so perhaps those could be handled together?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have decided to admit both documents, although we doubt their relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. As to Defence Exhibit 118 and 119, we have no objection, on a couple of conditions. The first one, in relation to 118, we just want to make sure that the date is clarified on the translation. On 118, the original, which is in Serbian, indicates a date of the 1st of January, 1991. On the translation, it's not clear if that's 1991 or 1992. So we just wanted to point that out, that the date should be '91, because the 1, it says 1 January --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two categories of those documents. One is the 1st January, 1991, the other one is 1st January, 1992. We just wanted to show the difference. That was the purpose of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. About this document you have just cited, so the date is '91 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on 118, it says situation on 1 January -- the date should be '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So it's not absolutely clear. And then as to both this exhibit and 119, we have no objection based on a similar document that we submitted being admitted, which would be Prosecutor's Exhibit 209. At that time, I think Mr. Fila had objected to it on the basis that these were not being admitted, and we agreed with that until we had seen the translations. So if the Prosecutor's document on the same issue is admitted, then we would have no objection to these being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, would you agree? Not to object to 209?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So both are admitted, also Prosecution Exhibit 209.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Then, as to 120 and 121, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As to Exhibits 122, 123, we would object to these. These appear to be listings of cease-fire violations. At the time that this issue was raised, the Prosecutor lodged an objection on the basis that if information was submitted in regard to cease-fires, that we would feel the necessity to rebut it, and at that point, the court had cut off any testimony on that issue. So we have not had an opportunity to rebut this. We had substantial material on cease-fire violations as well on the opposite side, and so that was the basis for this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We admit those documents, although again we doubt their relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me just explain. This is not the document on the cease-fire. This document, the first document, is not about the cease-fire, it's a letter to the Prime Minister of Croatia, Franjo Gregoric, that military property is being looted, 29 September, 1991. Not at the time when the cease-fire was on, but this is just general looting. The next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: To which document are you referring? 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. That's not during the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And 123 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: 123 is what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have already ruled that we admit both of them, although, as I say, we very much doubt their relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was my mistake. I had misread it so ... As to 124 and 125, we would object. This appears to be orders that are coming from the Croatian police asking for mobilisation, the second one in regard to protecting buildings of the US and other countries which were involved in the Persian Gulf conflict, and we fail to see the relevance of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We agree. They are not relevant. So they are not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And then from 126 on, I believe that all of those materials relate to the uniforms, and if that's the case, we would have no objection to those items being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Good. So they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honours, if Mr. Williamson would allow? Do I have to submit those documents now in five copies or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you just give one copy, we will provide copies to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have made them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you have four copies, even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I did make those copies. All the documents that have been admitted, just to make things go faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether there are any other matters relating to the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Regarding the matters yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the two videotapes that were sought to be tendered, they don't appear to have the -- oh, yes, they do. D156 and D157. We have looked at both of those, and we have no objection to them being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The supporting statements to the videos, 145 -- 154 and 145 -- 155, 154 and 155, we have no objection to those, Your Honour. They're merely the statements that admit the videos, so that they were ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the exhibit, the statement of Mr. Novakovic, 158 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- Your Honours, the position that we have on this is that the information about the drinking during the course of the interview is disputed by the investigator, and I have obtained a statement from the investigator setting out what he says the position was. Our position on it is that if this particular statement is to be admitted and our statement can be admitted alongside it on the record, we can see the two views of both this man and the investigator, and we'd have no objection on that basis. The problem we have, Your Honours, is that this suggestion, that they were drinking during the course of the interview, is a reflection upon the professional integrity of the officer, and he's an officer that is seconded to the Tribunal, he's not a U.N. employee as such, and we have wider interests of the government that supports his secondment. I would also be concerned if this matter is left unaddressed. So for that reason, we are anxious to ensure that if this allegation is made, which we don't wish to make an issue out of, frankly, we are most concerned that there is on the record a statement from the officer where it addresses the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I'm sorry to interrupt, but isn't there already evidence before the Tribunal, because he was cross-examined, as I recollect, about the drinking, and he said in terms that they weren't drinking, and I remember he was asked whether there was a bottle of whisky on the table, and he said not, but that afterwards they had gone to a restaurant, they had been taken to a restaurant, when Mr. Novakovic consumed a considerable quantity of alcohol and became incapacitated. That, as I recollect, was his evidence. So he has had a chance of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if -- I mean, that being the case then, perhaps my approach to it is wrong-footed, I should have just objected to this document going into evidence at all, because the issue has been addressed and dealt with. It has been raised in cross-examination, addressed, and dealt with. So if Your Honours are concerned about admitting a further statement, then that is the basis of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would first like to remove any suspicion from Mr. Curtis and also from me. Far be it from me to want to besmirch the name of Mr. Curtis. On the contrary. Mr. Novakovic said something to Witness Vasic, and Witness Vasic conveyed that to you. Whether Witness Novakovic said the truth or not, we don't know that. But neither Mr. Vasic nor Mr. Novakovic said that Mr. Curtis had been drinking, which would bring his reputation into question. They both said that he never had a drop of alcohol. But if this is a problem, it's up to you, as far as the statement is concerned, because Mr. Vasic already used the statement in his testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, Mr. Fila is right, because in a way, the main point of that witness was precisely, in these statements, to show that it was Mr. Novakovic who actually drank whisky or whatever while they were talking. This is your allegation. I agree, nobody has ever said that Mr. Curtis drank anything except probably coffee or soft drinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that the concern is, Your Honour, the suggestion that Mr. Novakovic -- a statement was taken from him in circumstances where it was known that he was intoxicated, and I believe that there was a suggestion that both of them had been drinking, but I accept Your Honour's point there, that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So, therefore, I wonder whether you could withdraw your objection to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I don't withdraw my objection. This is all irrelevant now because it has been dealt with in the course of the trial, in the cross-examination. It's not a matter for rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I mean, your objection to this document being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I do object to it, Your Honour, because it's irrelevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You do object to it because it's irrelevant. Our ruling is that this document shall not be admitted into evidence because it is not relevant. I am speaking of D158 and D158A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to the evidence about Witness Q, I note Your Honours' ruling on that in relation to the documents, so I'm not addressing that, but we were able to, during the course of the evening, to obtain a statement from Witness Q as to his recollection of the events. I have it available. I can provide it to my friends as to the position. I'm not submitting it in rebuttal or -- could this be shown to the Defence, please? -- to what has been raised by Mr. Fila in that statement, but it does address the matters that were raised in the examination of the witness, and I'm not making application to tender it, but I invite Mr. Fila to tender it so that the record indicates precisely what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very gladly, but I need to have a look. Maybe we could discuss the issue of sentencing, you could discuss the issue of sentencing while we're having a look at this, so as not to waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. At the coffee break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next matter, Your Honour, was the judgement of the court in Osijek which is Exhibit 160. We still have not received a translation of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I received it this morning. I have the translation here, so maybe I can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have a look at that, and while Mr. Fila is looking at the other one, we could look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So later on. We will come back to D160 later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's all the matters I think that are outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, have you got any matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, yes. I apologise, Mr. Niemann, but we do have one more thing to discuss. In the meantime, we have received the report of the Dutch police regarding the tape. I would now like to submit this document because I would like to remind the Trial Chamber we still haven't had your decision whether we need the person who wrote the report here or whether we can just admit the report without hearing the testimony of the person who prepared it. That's the position of the Defence counsel. Once you see it, you will see that this is actually the case. That would be a better idea. So, please, if this could be distributed? While I read this document, maybe my colleagues from the Prosecution could read this document also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: When you said, Mr. Fila, when you said you were wondering whether we would like to ask the person who wrote the report to come here, you were referring to the police officer, Dutch police officer, who wrote the report you are now tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because I asked the Prosecutor to have the document admitted without this person having to come here, but Mr. Niemann wanted to have a look at the report before making a decision or taking a stand on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We also need some time because -- as soon as we are given this report, we will look into this matter. Now, I wonder whether we could put off all these matters until the coffee break so as not to waste time. We start with the two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Professor Gudjonsson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for our witness, may I ask you whether you have received the reports of the medical officer and the confidential report of the commanding officer of the detention unit? It has been circulated. I hope both parties have received those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I address the court for just a second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: -- before the witness arrives? We are in receipt of a two-page report by the witness that's coming now, Dr. Gudjonsson, that is dated June 12th of 1998. I'm assuming that Your Honours have that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: The question I have before this witness testifies is that the witness renders an opinion on page 1 in a paragraph that is entitled No. 2, which is the bottom, the last paragraph on page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: In reading that paragraph, it appears to me that the doctor is commenting on a section of Dr. Petrovic's report. When I looked at the transcript of the testimony of Dr. Petrovic, I noted at page 3308 that Dr. Petrovic was foreclosed from testifying about the identification procedures; in other words, to discuss the testimony of the witnesses -- I think I'm not supposed to mention their names, if I'm correct, but you know the two witnesses I'm speaking about. So her testimony was limited to her work with Mr. Dokmanovic, his mental state, and so on. What I am asking the court now, and maybe I should have asked the Prosecutors beforehand, and I apologise for that, is whether this doctor, this particular witness, will actually go into discussion of the topic of paragraph 2, in other words, the subject matter. I would think that that witness should be foreclosed from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour. We're not going to raise it. It was addressed in the report because -- I don't know whether at that stage the -- no, it hadn't. It was addressed in the report, but it's certainly not a matter which I'll be asking the witness about, and if I seek to tender his report, I will ask Your Honours to disregard the second paragraph in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: In that view, in that view, Your Honours, with the agreement of Mr. Niemann, I feel now a little -- well, let me explain it to you. Because Dr. Najman, whose report you have, has also discussed to some degree, in response to this paragraph, the testimony of those witnesses, I'm assuming what's proper, and then the problematic thing is that she names these witnesses, and I'm not sure how we can cure that because I think her report may already be with you, at least with the Prosecution. I'm not sure if it's with Your Honours. We can either block it, or the only other way to cure that, Your Honours, maybe would be to have a closed session in regard to Dr. Najman's testimony, so that the identification of those two witnesses are not released, and I'm asking the court for guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware of them being confidential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They testified in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Then it's fine. Then I'm raising a problem that is not a problem. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As for it being mentioned in their report, Your Honours, likewise, presumably it can be disregarded in the same way as we would ask that their paragraph 2 be disregarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: As to Dr. Gudjonsson, Dr. Najman may have comments about Dr. Wagenaar, but that's a different matter. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Could you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor Gudjonsson, do you hold a master of science in clinical psychology and a doctor of philosophy from the University of Surrey?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you a lecturer in psychology, a senior lecturer in psychology, and now are you a reader in forensic psychology at the Institute of Psychiatry at Kings College in London?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you also an honorary top grade clinical psychologist to the Maudsley and Bethlem Royal Hospital?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's more commonly referred described nowadays as a "B" grade which is the most senior grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you affiliated with several professional bodies such as the British Psychological Society and the Magistrates Association, and are you a chartered clinical psychologist?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your scientific career, have you focused almost exclusively on forensic and criminological psychology?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your career, have you pioneered the empirical measurement of interrogative suggestibility, and are the two suggestibility scales that you have developed now widely used in forensic practice as well as in research?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: That's correct. I also developed a test of compliance which has been published along with the other two tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you also recently been involved in the construction of a theoretical model of interrogative suggestibility which is guiding current research internationally?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you involved in a long-term research project on the phenomena of false confessions and an investigation into the mental state and psychological characteristics of suspects detained at police stations for questioning?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does your research also relate to reliability of evidence and, in this respect, have you studied the nature and characteristics of suggestibility, memory, confabulation in psychiatric patients?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you also conduct research into amnesia after an offence?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have over 170 peer-reviewed scientific publications, including publications on homicide, lie detection, the attitude of offenders towards their crime, the credibility of witness accounts, and false confessions?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Have you provided evidence in over 800 criminal cases, 140 of which you have testified, including a number of high-profile cases colloquially known as the Guildford 4, the Birmingham 6, the Tottenham 3, and the Cardiff 3?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to now show you a document.

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Just to not have any misunderstanding, with regard to the 140 cases where I've testified, I've testified in court in just over 140 or just about 140 criminal cases. Now, seven have been in the Court of Appeal. I did not testify directly or in person with regard to the Guildford 4 or the Birmingham 6. I provided reports which were used to re-open these cases and were used, but not with my regard to my having to testify in these two cases in person in the Court of Appeal in London. That's just to correct in case there are any misperceptions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, the document that is now shown to you, is that a copy of your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: This is an abbreviated version of my CV. I've got a much more extensive version, but this is just a brief version, and it doesn't actually list all my publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked 264.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor Gudjonsson, in June of this year, were you approached by Mr. Milner of the Office of the Prosecutor with a request to evaluate the expert report by Dr. Vera Petrovic on Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic and to comment on the accuracy of the conclusions contained in that report?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After accepting that request, did you subsequently study the report of Dr. Petrovic, and did you come to a number of findings which you laid down in an outline of your preliminary views which you sent to Mr. Milner?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In preparing your outline, did you rely on any information other than the report of Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: No, only on the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'd now like to show you this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked 265.

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, this is a faxed copy of my report. I actually have the original if you need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think this one will be satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this but, as discussed previously, might paragraph 2 be disregarded by the court, and it's not sought to be tendered. Dr. Gudjonsson, in her report, Dr. Petrovic maintains that the personality features of Mr. Dokmanovic, his mental state, his behaviour after the arrest, and the lack of aggression in his earlier life do not correspond to his alleged behaviour at Ovcara. Do you agree with that finding?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: No, I do not because I do not think that these characteristics say anything about the kind of behaviour that may occur in wartime and that commonly occurs in wartime. There have been many books and many research papers done in this area, and it clearly shows that what we're dealing with is group behaviour. We're dealing not just with an ordinary criminal behaviour where you typically find a history, a previous history of violence. We're dealing with something different in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What, in this respect, is the significance of the research carried out by Stanley Milgram in the 1970s?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Well, basically, Stanley Milgram, I actually have a copy of his book here. That was a very influential book, because after the war, people were concerned about the extent to which the Germans were engaged in killing the Jews, pretty ordinary Germans who had no history of previous violence towards anybody who were engaged in some horrendous acts. And books were written about this, and Stanley Milgram produced a book in 1974 called "Obedience to Authority" where he did research that basically demonstrated that it is very easy to engage people in horrendous acts and inhumane acts when people are ordered to do so by a person in authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, I will object to the answer to this question. I ask that you strike it from the record, because it is not based on any scientific research done by this witness. It also seems to indicate that the witness is repeating a work of someone else dealing with another historical period and, finally, is not based on the review or the assessment of what may have been done in the instant case that you're judging. So I think that he is not giving us a scientific opinion, and he is here as an expert witness as opposed to somebody who is here to discuss history or other works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kostic, the whole point is that he's an expert. And as an expert, he is entitled to refer to other works which have been produced. The whole point of his giving evidence is that he gives us his expertise, and that expertise includes the knowledge which he has of the works of others which, it seems to me, he's perfectly entitled to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I may add one small comment, since I happen to have read this book. I think that either you give details about actually what the book is about or it does not make sense to comment on that book.

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I can certainly give details. A number of experiments were done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In a succinct way, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We would like to rule that as a matter of principle, of course, expert witnesses are entitled to refer to books written by other scholars. However, with regard to the specific book in question, we really wonder to what extent it may be relevant to this issue under discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In particular, do the reactions of Mr. Dokmanovic to his arrest and subsequent behaviour in custody tell you anything about his propensity to act as alleged in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. There is nothing there that would give an indication one way or the other about his involvement in the alleged atrocities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in her report, Dr. Petrovic attaches great value to the remarks made by Mr. Dokmanovic recorded on the videotape, Exhibit D2, and she quotes one particular quote from Mr. Dokmanovic where he says "The world has never seen anything like it, not even that place Arnhem looked like this ... the immense grief..." I think you've been referred to that. What, in your opinion, is the relevance of these remarks for a psychological assessment of Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty is that it could mean many different things, because we don't know what it means, and I think it's only a question of speculation. I think it's better not to be reading anything particular into it, because it could be interpreted in so many different ways. I mean, one interpretation might be that he suddenly realised the enormity of what had happened or it may be that it was used in order to excuse what he had done. I'm not assuming guilt or innocence. I'm just saying there are many different ways of interpreting what is being said, and it would be better not to speculate about exactly what it means, because we don't know from a scientific perspective what exactly it does mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in the analysis section of her report, Dr. Petrovic identifies a number of personality traits of Mr. Dokmanovic, and she lists anxiety, perfectionism, obsessiveness, dependiveness (sic) depression, paranoia and other traits that are characteristic of a neurotic person. In your opinion, does this material available justify that conclusion, that Mr. Dokmanovic possesses these traits?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, as far as I can see from the report, there was an extensive clinical evaluation. There was psychological tests that were actually administered which are typically described as psychological rather than psychiatric tests, but the tests were administered. On the basis of what I've seen in the report about the test findings, I do think the conclusions about these characteristics are justified on the basis of the assessment being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your opinion, does the presence of these characteristics say anything about, whether either positive or negative, the propensity of Mr. Dokmanovic to commit the alleged offences?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: No, they don't. It is very dangerous to be taking those characteristics and speculating about what he may or may have not done in wartime. It bears no relationship at all. There is no scientific evidence to indicate that these characteristics, one way or the other, have any bearing on the issue. Your Honour, it is distracting, the extensive conversation going on whilst I'm listening and speaking. It is distracting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask Mr. Fila to be so kind as to refrain from talking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you are a doctor of psychology; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You have reviewed the reports of Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You have also reviewed the attachments to her report, have you not?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And the attachments include, among other things, a battery of tests; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Commonly known as an "MMPI"; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Just to explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was going to ask you if you would explain what an MMPI testing procedure is?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: The MMPI test that's used in this case is not the standard MMPI used in the scientific field generally. It is an abbreviated test. I've never seen an abbreviated version of the MMPI used in this way before. The MMPI was a test that was developed in the 1940s, and it was then restandardised about 15 years ago and changed the name to the MMPI-2, and it's been revised. It contains 567 items. It basically has three validity scales and ten clinical scales. And the validity scales indicate to what extent the responses can be relied upon as being reliable and valid. And the clinical scales monitor a number of different clinical conditions. The last scale, which is social introversion, is actually not a clinical scale but, rather, a personality scale. So there's an overlap between this being a clinical measure and it being a personality measure. It's really a combination of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: But it's commonly used, is it not?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, extensively used, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You've used it yourself in your practice, have you not?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: I've used it extensively. I've also conducted research using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Now, in addition to using the standard tests, one of the other ways that expert witnesses like yourself reach a conclusion is through interviews with the subject; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And the reports that you have reviewed indicates that Dr. Petrovic had spent quite a bit of time in the personal interviews of Mr. Dokmanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And that is something that you would also do in your practice; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: The difference, I suppose, between your practice and that of Dr. Petrovic is that she is a medical doctor, correct, a psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: So she may have some different insight than you do; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And, of course, she deals with the administration of medications; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that the best way to reach a judgement or an analysis in regard to a patient is to have a number of personal interviews and observations of the patient?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Without that, you really cannot reach a good analysis of the problems, and I'm simplifying this, correct, as opposed to a diagnosis, but the problems that the patient has?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: In addition, if you support your personal interviews and observations with the standard testing procedure, that is also helpful?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And then if you are capable of reviewing other documents -- in a criminal case, of course, you would talk about the complaints or the statements of witnesses -- that also helps, does it not?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Then, finally, if you have an opportunity, as in this case Dr. Petrovic did, to discuss the subject with other people who have observed Mr. Dokmanovic, such as the warden of the prison and others, that is also a helpful tool in your final diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Are you referring to Mr. McFaden?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: For example, for example.

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Is there anything else that you can think of that Dr. Petrovic may have been able to do or should have done in terms of considering all of the documentation and information in reaching her diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: I have no criticism of Dr. Petrovic with regard to her assessment as such. My only observations are about the conclusions she draws from her findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm assuming that what you have done is to review the report of Dr. Petrovic and then review the allegations; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Well, only the allegations as far as they are documented in her report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And you have then assumed next that if the allegations are true, then her diagnosis is false; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: No, no, no. I have to correct here. We're not talking about her diagnosis. She has made a diagnosis, and that's a clinical diagnosis, that this man has got certain clinical problems, including depression and anxiety and paranoid tendencies. That's the diagnosis. The inferences that are drawn from the diagnosis about his behaviour or how he might react in another setting is not a diagnosis. Those are interpretations. So I just want to make clear, this is not a diagnosis. These are her inferences that she has drawn about his behaviour, what he might behave like in other settings, based on the clinical findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: She has done that on the basis of what's in the record; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree with that. Yes, she's drawn on her assessment and on the documents that she has seen in this case, in addition to the people with whom she has spoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Now, you would have preferred, would you not, in rendering your opinion the same ability as Dr. Petrovic has had, the ability to interview Mr. Dokmanovic, the ability to interview Mr. McFaden, things of that nature? Would you not have preferred that?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: It depends what my purpose is. If I had been asked to do a clinical evaluation of him, I would have said, "Yes, I do need to see him," and I would insist on seeing him if I was asked to perform a clinical evaluation. It is extremely unwise to perform a clinical evaluation of somebody you haven't seen. What I've been asked to do here is to comment on the report, which is not unusual for one to do. I'm not carrying out a clinical evaluation. I'm just commenting on the report and the conclusions in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Now, to understand your testimony then, you feel that Dr. Petrovic did not have sufficient information in order to reach her conclusions?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about what I feel. I'm talking about what I know. There's a difference. Now, what I know is the conclusions she has drawn are unjustified because there are no scientific bases on which she can draw those inferences on the basis of the clinical findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And that is your opinion; correct?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: That's my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And yours, of course, differs from Dr. Petrovic, does it not?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Petrovic has presented to evidence to substantiate her conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Have we talked about all of your opinions that you have in regard to this case so far?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You have no other opinions to give in regard to Dr. Petrovic's report?

utterances.speaker: GISLI GUDJONSSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing in re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, I assume there's no objection to the witness being released? Professor, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence in court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We're wondering whether we could -- we thought we could go on and call the other witness before the coffee break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, because the next witness has some relationship to this witness, I would appreciate a short break just to be able to consult with the witness with a view that maybe I can shorten her testimony. I apologise for that, but I think it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Judge May was wondering whether we had received a report from your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic does have it, and if you would like, we could hand it up before, if there's no objection from our friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, all right, why not? In any case, I think it's quite appropriate for us to take a break, say, a 15-minute break. Is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: That is sufficient, Your Honour. The other thing I would like to add, if there's no objection again all the way around, we would give you the CV, curriculum vitae, of the witness and the report so that you have the whole packet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Let us, first of all then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might we also get a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I, in no way, meant to exclude Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Let us, first of all, receive the document and then we will take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The CV will be marked D163 and the report D164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we rise now and we reconvene in, let's say, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do have one witness to offer to the court. I hope she is on her way. This is Dr. Najman or -- Mr. Fila has a question whether -- he would like to ask you about the document that you had talked about earlier this morning having to do with a witness and rebuttal testimony of a witness, I think it's Q, I think it's Witness Q. I will let Mr. Fila talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the matters we had decided to put off for discussion so that the parties could come to some sort of agreement. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, it was Mr. Fila, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, this was for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't understand the nature of this document, Your Honour. I don't know why it was given to me, the statement made by Witness Q yesterday -- today. I'm a bit disappointed because the OTP acknowledged, as my only quality, my speed. That is the only contribution I have made. That's what they say in their closing statement. However, in order to earn a compliment from Mr. Niemann that I contribute to the truth, I am not opposed to having this document included where Mr. Niemann deems it fit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, and Mr. Fila may have misunderstood what I was meaning, but there was -- our case, of course, is in rebuttal, but I wasn't seeking to tender it, I was merely inviting Mr. Fila to do so, if he felt it appropriate to do so, because it was a statement taken of the witness in relation to a document he tendered. I invited him to do it. It's entirely a matter for him as to whether he wants to do it or not, and if Mr. Fila is prepared to do it, I have given it to him, and I invite him to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So Mr. Niemann is asking you whether you would be prepared to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm not opposed to it. I cannot tender somebody else's document, though, but I am not opposed to Mr. Niemann doing it, and I agreed to that, as I have already told you. An additional document will do us no harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Mr. Fila has no objections and Your Honours have no objections, then I will tender it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And if Mr. Fila doesn't have it, then it might be given to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What about the report of the Dutch police officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no objection to that being tendered in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And also the judgement from Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have read that, Your Honours, and we cannot see how it's relevant, having read the Statement of Reasons of the court. It's not a matter that we say touches on any of the issues that are before Your Honours for decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Fila put it out yesterday that it was for sentencing purposes that he was tendering that document, the judgement, the Osijek judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Sentencing, yes. Your Honour, in my system, and also, I believe, in Mr. Niemann's system, it is not all the same whether someone was convicted and then is being re-tried. That's the point. That is why this judgement has been presented. In other words, that Mr. Dokmanovic does not have a criminal record. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In that case, of course, Your Honour, I have no objections. I didn't understand the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It was clarified yesterday by Mr. Fila. All right. So it is admitted into evidence. We are speaking, of course, of the Osijek judgement, and also the Dutch police report. What about the number -- the Dutch police report is tendered by the Defence, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. So the court's documents will be marked as D160, and the other document D162, the report of the Dutch police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we could receive a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is very simple. It is an additional check on what I have already provided from Yugoslavia, that is, whether Mr. Dokmanovic's voice is heard at given points in time or not, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was one other matter. It related to the documents that we had received from the archives of the Security Council yesterday, being the letter and attachment to the letter by Mr. Mesic. Mr. Fila was going to look at it overnight because it was, in fact, a new document and he hadn't seen it, and so I don't know what his position on that is now. It was Exhibit P108.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That was a document in the Croatian language, if I'm not mistaken -- I mean in the Serbian language. It is easier for me. I'm a faster reader of Serbo Croatian than English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was not. It was in the English language, Your Honour. It was written by -- apparently -- in both languages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. Since you accepted the document on the attacks on barracks, I accepted this document too because it's the same subject matter. That's it. Yes, it's all right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection. All right. What number has it got?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's document 108A. Correction. It's 108/1 because there was already a translation of the 108 so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether you could bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Would you state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Ana Najman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Make sure that you speak into the microphone that's in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: All right. Ana Najman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Ms. Najman, keep in mind that the court has your CV. What I would like to do is to just add or explain portions of your CV. Let me ask you a question. That will be easiest, I think. On your CV, there is a period of time, 1977 on, which talks about a specialisation in medical and clinical psychology at the medical faculty in Belgrade. Would you please explain that to the court or elaborate?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes. In Yugoslavia, there are basic bachelor studies of psychology after which one gets a bachelor's degree of a psychologist, and after a certain time of practice, a psychologist has the right to work with patients. There are also studies at the faculty of medicine in the field of clinical psychology, and after these three-year studies, one gets the title of a specialist in clinical psychology. That means formally a higher degree of education. After three years of studies, such a person can also work with patients, that is to say, can acquire a lot more experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: In addition, on the second page of your CV, where there's a year 1988, we have an entry which says: "Registered as forensic medicine expert with the Ministry of Justice of Republic of Serbia." First of all, tell us whether you are still so registered and again explain that particular portion of your CV?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: This is still valid. I'm still registered as a forensic medicine expert so I am still such an expert, and I'm actively involved in this line of work as I work in the gaol hospital in Belgrade, that is to say, I worked there for ten years, so I have had practical experience in addition to the education I have received, and that is why I registered as a forensic medicine expert. What is customary in our country is to have a commission of experts together with a psychiatrist in all fields of criminal law and civil law and also psychological examination is compulsory, according to our law, for all persons who have committed crimes and also for juvenile delinquents and also perpetrators and victims who are younger adults. Younger adults are persons who have not yet turned 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Do you testify as a matter of course in the courts of your country?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: What is the frequency and also if you are able to give me some estimation as to how many times you have done that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Approximately three or four times per week for all cases where first a written report is submitted to the court and then there is oral questioning, and the number of cases has certainly exceeded 400, 500 over this number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You also do work with patients of your own. Do you see patients on some kind of a basis?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. For two years now, I have been working at the psychiatry ward in Belgrade, and I also worked in the prison hospital at the ward for patients who were perpetrators of grave crimes and who, due to their illness, were being treated in hospital. That was the so-called warfare psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You have also indicated, and I'm not sure if it's on your CV, but you have told me and I would like to have you explain to the court, your experience in the area of the identification process, in other words, the psychology of identification. Can you tell us about your experience in that area?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: In Belgrade, at the faculty of philosophy, there is a laboratory for experimental psychology, and I attended a postgraduate course there and I cooperated with them, and I continue my cooperation with them. During my expertise, we have also made evaluations, assessments related to perception identification, the process of thought, disorders of thought, and of other cognitive functions, so from that field I have had quite a bit of experience too in continuity that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Have you testified in the courts of your country on issues of identification and related issues?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: On numerous occasions?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Not that often, but often enough, and only in relation to criminal law, so criminal cases prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: The criminal courts are the courts which generally have the identification process issue?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to just ask you a very limited question about the report of Dr. Petrovic. Have you reviewed the report of Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Have you read the attachments to the report?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Did you review a section which is commonly referred to as an MMPI testing result or results?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the MMPI and the other tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: What was the type of MMPI test that was administered to Mr. Dokmanovic by Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: In this expertise on Mr. Dokmanovic, the MMPI test was carried out, 201, that is the abbreviated version, that is the version that is used in Yugoslavia and which is standardised in terms of our own population in the 1980s. So this is a test which is absolutely considered to be verified in clinical practice and valid for our population. As far as psychological measurement instruments are concerned, I wish to note that they have to be tested on the population to which they're being administered. You will allow me just a brief explanation. There are different characteristics, for example, between the American population and the Yugoslav population, so this is just by way of comparison, but that is why this standardisation is made and that is why it has to be verified in terms of the population where it is administered. So this was standardised on our population, this test.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Do you use that particular test in your practice?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I use it every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You're satisfied it's an appropriate tool for your work and for your analysis and for your testimony in court?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to change topics and ask you if you have reviewed a report which was submitted by the Prosecution of an expert witness called Willem Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You have that in front of you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You have also submitted to the court, or through us you have submitted to the court, your own analyses and review of Dr. Wagenaar's findings in his report; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: You have your report in front of you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Because the court has both one of the expert witness's reports, which is Dr. Wagenaar, and also has yours, what I'm going to ask you is to turn to page 4 of your report because we may be able to shorten your testimony this morning. I don't think anybody here has an objection to that. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: On page 4, there is a section which is entitled "Recognition"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: What is contained under those two paragraphs is your analysis of Dr. Wagenaar's report; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Do you have, in addition to what you wrote, would you wish to highlight or comment on your report in regard to that particular expertise of Dr. Wagenaar, and if so, please do so now.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I just wish to clarify one point which was certainly written in this report too, and that is that I fully agree with the expert opinion presented by Mr. Wagenaar. It is certainly based on all the scientific postulates of psychology, notably in the period of perception. What I wish to highlight, though, is the fact that Mr. Wagenaar, as he also wrote, had in his report as a basic premise a general position, a general principle of perception that occurs with people. He did not bear in mind the specific situation, the statements of the mentioned witnesses, and he did not bear in mind the situation in which the perception took place. So he considered perception in so-called general ideal conditions, not in specific conditions, and that is what I wrote here too. When his postulates, which are absolutely correct and which are adopted and there is nothing to be added to them, really, are applied to a specific situation, though, then his opinion, in a way, has to be modified because we have to take into account the specific situation and the effect of all other factors on human perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to add anything else in regard to the "Recognition" portion?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: At this point, this would do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Then let's turn to the next section of Dr. Wagenaar's report. It is entitled "Remembering Uniforms." If I'm not mistaken, what you have done is to key your comments to the key in Dr. Wagenaar's report; is that correct? Would you now, first of all, give us a general statement about your -- not feeling, your expert opinion about the doctor's general statement about uniforms, and then we'll go into the subsections?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: What I have said previously relating to the general view also applies to the recognition of uniforms. So Mr. Wagenaar, in his first paragraph, discussed in general the recognition of uniforms. In this case, I will call it "form." And then he went on to discuss in paragraphs (a) through (h), separately, each of the situations. I also discussed this, but not in general terms, but I linked it with the testimonies of the two witnesses which I have had the chance to see. So that is how I formed my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Part of your opinion is based on reviewing the statements of the two witnesses in question?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: And now I think -- I'm sorry, I interrupted you. Did you want to proceed to section (a) and discuss that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, if the Trial Chamber allows, we can discuss this paragraph (a).

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think it's the best way to do it. It's the most orderly. So why don't you go ahead?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: What I would like to stress is the fact that both witnesses mentioned the uniform in their first statement, so there were no additional questions that was the result of their perceptive act of what they saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, my understanding, Your Honours, is that we weren't going to delve into the question of analysis of what the witnesses said and Dr. Wagenaar certainly didn't do that, he spoke in general terms only, and in my submission, this goes well beyond appropriate rejoinder because it wasn't discussed by Dr. Wagenaar and it's inappropriate for this witness to discuss it; and in any event, Your Honours had ruled, when dealing with Dr. Petrovic's report, that dealing with the witnesses themselves specifically, it was a matter for Your Honours and not for the experts to testify on. So I object to any discussion going beyond general principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. No dishonour to the court. I have reviewed Dr. Wagenaar's report, and pursuant to that, I think this particular witness was retained. I thought that it would be fair for her to comment on anything that's in the record in regard to this identification issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, anything which is in the report, in Dr. Wagenaar's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: But she cannot comment on Dr. Wagenaar's report unless she goes into a concrete discussion, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I confirm that it would not be appropriate to go into any details and to discuss in particular the testimony of those two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I just have to understand the ruling, Your Honour, I'm not being difficult, because -- is what you're saying is that you're foreclosing discussion of the two witnesses because there was no other testimony by these witnesses? I don't understand the ruling, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This is a rejoinder witness. You are calling this witness in rejoinder, and it's rejoinder to Professor Wagenaar's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, the witness should confine herself to touching upon those issues which have been raised by Professor Wagenaar in his written report which has now been admitted into evidence. Therefore, she should not touch upon matters which were not dealt with by Professor Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: So that your ruling is -- you said rejoinder. I think I probably understand it as a rebuttal or surrebuttal or rejoinder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We call it rebuttal and rejoinder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you. What you are saying then, therefore, because Dr. Wagenaar did not mention the witnesses specifically, that you would foreclose me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to understand the ruling because I'm unclear. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: What I need you to do then, Dr. Najman, is without discussing the testimony of the other witnesses, I do need you to comment generally on whether you agree with the opinion of Dr. Wagenaar on the issue of remembering uniforms or do you not agree, or do you feel that Dr. Wagenaar has, in some way, omitted something or, in your opinion, gave an opinion that you differ with? So if you can do that in general terms, I think that might satisfy the court.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I fully agree with the explanation given by Dr. Wagenaar. In general terms, it is absolutely based on the laws of perception. What I wish to add, however, also in general terms, is that perception of colour, that form is a primary principle in every act of perception in human beings. I would also like to stress that it alters under the influence of certain factors, internal and external. I would just like to add, if the Trial Chamber allows me to, I would like to stress the effect of internal factors which, in this case, are deemed to be more important. These are psychological, motivational, emotional factors and factors of situation or the circumstances in which the person finds himself in. Psychological factors are extremely important for the way in which we perceive things. Without the influence of those psychological factors, we have the perception which is, so to speak, conditionally speaking, "normal." If the effect of psychological or emotional factors prevails, our perception changes. This also relates to -- just to make things short -- to emotional, social factors, and physiological factors as well. I would also like to mention those. First of all, we mean certain physiological circumstances that a human being can find himself in, whether one is hungry or well-fed; also stress, the effect of stress can also be deemed physiological but also psychological factor. But as we all know, the biology and physiology of the human being reacts in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Dr. Wagenaar's report also talks about colours, and he mentions the colour blue, and you also have in your report talked about that colour. Can you explain that to the court, the importance of that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, this is also a principle which has been established as existing in perception. The primary colours are very important in the perception. What we see the first moment is colour, form, and shape. In every human organism, there is the biological factor which regulates the constancy of our perception. For instance, we don't see this colour in a different tone, hue, if the external factors that affect us are minimal. So there is a certain constancy of perception, and it is extremely important, because due to that, our lives have been made easier. Because the perception of colour, for instance, or of form does not change as fast as the outside stimuli can change. So there is a certain biological regulator in the human perception regulating both the colour, the shape, and the form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: My last question: Dr. Wagenaar also talks in one portion of his report about the wearing of insignia, and you also talk about insignia. Can you explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: All right. The perception of details belongs to the secondary process of perceptive experience. So the primary, as I said, is the perception of colour, shape and form; and the secondary is the perception of details. The secondary process is much more influenced by those internal and external factors. And we cannot overlook that because, to a great extent, the perception of those details may differ from one man to another. It does not mean that the stimulus that they perceived, the object, was different. Their internal experience was different. It differed from man to man and, of course, the factor of personality which is not to be overlooked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Najman, do you know Professor Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know of his work?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know of the work of Dr. Wagenaar? Have you ever read any of his material that he has produced?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know that he has a reputation of being one of the most eminent experts in the world on the question of identification? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In fact, I think it's generally accepted in international circles that there's probably only one or two other people who could profess to have the same high degree of competence as Dr. Wagenaar in this particular area; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said that you appeared in courts in your own country. Have you ever appeared in any other courts, apart from those in the former Yugoslavia, before and testified?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Do you mean outside of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you appear, can you tell us what is the bulk of the work that you do? What are you primarily concerned with when you testify in courts in your country?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: My testimony before the court is the result of my previous work with the person I examined. I also have insight into the court record, a psychological evaluation, then I write the report, and only then do I testify before the court giving similar answers as I do here. On the one hand, we have the Defence asking questions and, on the other, we have the Prosecutor asking questions and, very often, the Trial Chamber itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, am I right in saying that the vast bulk of what you do in your own courts is to make a psychological assessment, presumably, in most cases, of the person who is being accused of a crime, and then report to the court on your opinion of that accused person's psychological state; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that, however, you have given evidence on occasion on identification issues; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but if I have your permission, I would like to note, as regards the identification in Yugoslavia, the very narrow, specific problem is much less important. It is usually viewed in a broader sense, in the sense of the whole case, in the context of the whole case. So it's not a separate item.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The issue that Dr. Wagenaar has reported on in his report would strike you as being somewhat unusual in terms of what you would generally do in the courts of your own country; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, you could say that. Because in addition to the general part that Dr. Wagenaar discussed, which we also do, we link it to the specific case under review, so that could constitute the difference. This is what I presented in my written report. I also apply this to the specific case, if that's what you were asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say that the MMPI test in Yugoslavia, number 201, I think, is especially adopted for the former Yugoslavia. Does it have any international recognition outside of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Of course. It's the same test that Mr. Gudjonsson talked about. In its original version, it has 567 questions; in its abbreviated versions, 201 questions. In our country, we also apply the full version, but this form, the 201 form, which has been applied here, is the standardised test, standardised to the Yugoslav population. What does that mean? The standardisation of a test means that it is applied to a large number of people from various regions using specific statistical methods. Certain conclusions are made, and then on the basis of that, the conclusion is reached that this test is valid, that the result achieved corresponds to the purpose and the objective for which it has been applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before you set out to comment upon the report of Dr. Wagenaar, did you make contact with him at all?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any reason why you didn't contact him?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No, no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kostic?
