utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Were you told by anyone that you had to contact Dr. Wagenaar or that it was necessary or that it was desirable?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I have no other questions of this witness. The only thing I would like to do is to move the Exhibits D163, D164 and D165 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Our position on that, Your Honours, is we have no objection, provided the conditions that were discussed before, namely, reference to the witnesses, are not regarded as part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. So we will disregard those parts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I have absolutely no disagreement with that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. It will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Najman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume there's no objection to the witness being released. Dr. Najman, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think we have now reached the stage where we should come to the closing statements, and I wonder whether Mr. Niemann is prepared to make his closing statement on behalf of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If Your Honours just excuse me while I just prepare myself. If Your Honours please. Your Honours, I have provided you with a copy of our closing address. The matters pertaining to the legal aspects of the discussion will be matters that I will address, and when it comes to a discussion of the facts of the case, my colleague, Mr. Williamson, will address Your Honours on those factual issues. Your Honours, the written submission that I have provided largely covers many of the points that I'd wish to make. It wasn't my intention, unless I can assist Your Honours in any of these matters, to actually go into that written submission. As with many legal issues, at times they can be a little tedious to have read to you, if Your Honours have had the opportunity to read it. So I'm not going to subject Your Honours to that. So there are some peripheral matters which I would like to address, and there are some central matters which I will go to which may bear some repetition or explanation. Your Honours, of course, if there are any matters that I can assist you with arising out of the submissions that I have made, particularly in relation to the legal questions, then I sincerely hope that I can assist Your Honours with those matters. Your Honours, the Prosecution and the Defence have now reached the conclusion of their part of the case, and it now turns to you to examine the facts and the law to be applied. Your Honours' role is not an easy one because not only must you deal with complex legal issues, but you must perform one of the more difficult tasks that have to be performed in a criminal trial, and that is to decide the issues of fact. In those jurisdictions where there is a jury of 12 ordinary citizens to deal with the questions of fact, the Trial Judge is somewhat relieved of that burden. But one of the aspects of a trial before a jury is that the Trial Judge invariably instructs the jury to apply their common sense when it comes to a decision on the facts and on a determination of the guilt or innocence of an accused person. Your Honours, the issue of determining guilt or innocence, according to common sense, in our submission, should be no different whether the tribunal, in fact, be an ordinary tribunal of citizens or a tribunal of trained lawyers. It's common, Your Honours, in a jury trial for Prosecutors to explain to the jury the roles played by the various parts of the court. This is because one can expect that ordinary laymen may not understand all of the different roles that are played. But I'm not sure that it's inappropriate for us in this Tribunal to also look at the various roles played by the parties and, on occasion, to remind ourselves of the various functions that need to be formed. It's interesting that in a trial with a jury, for example, Prosecutors are at pains to emphasise that the Trial Judge is the final arbiter of the law. And while it is for the jury to decide issues of fact, it is for the Judge to decide questions of law. Prosecutors often say to juries that if the jury hears two versions of the law, one from the Prosecution and one from the Judge, that they must and they are bound to accept the view of the law that is put to them by the Trial Judge. Why do I say this and why do I refer to this? Because, Your Honours, it is important to emphasise the reasons behind this, the reasons being that it's important that in a proceedings where juries are present to emphasise that the Prosecution plays a role in the case which is slightly different to that of the Defence and which is in support of the system of justice itself, such that when it comes to any issue of dispute that may be seen to confuse a jury on questions of law, the Prosecution make it clear that there is to be no dispute, that the Trial Judge is the Judge that determines that issue. And so the jury is not left to trouble themselves with these matters. They are there. And so to that extent, the Judge and the Prosecution stand together, and the Prosecution is in support of the court and the system of justice itself. Your Honours, if I may refer to what I think has probably become a classic definition of the role of the Prosecution as was formulated by a committee in the United Kingdom known as the Farquharson Committee in 1986. Your Honours, I pause to refer to this because I think it is useful that, in discussing the various roles to be played, the role of the Prosecution be clearly emphasised and stated. I do and I quote from that report. In the Farquharson report in its introductory paragraphs, it is stated that: "There is no doubt that the obligations on Prosecution counsel are different from those of counsel instructed for the Defence in a criminal case or of counsel instructed in civil matters. His or her duties are wider both to the court and to the public at large. Furthermore, having regard to his duty to present the case for the Prosecution fairly to the jury, he has a greater independence of those instructing him than that enjoyed by other counsel. It is well known to every practitioner that counsel for the Prosecution must conduct his case moderately, albeit firmly. He must not strive unfairly to obtain a conviction. He must not press his case beyond the limits which the evidence permits. He must not invite the jury to convict on evidence which, in his own judgement, no longer sustains the charges laid in the indictment. If the evidence of a witness is undermined or severely blemished in the course of cross-examination, Prosecution counsel must not present him to the jury as worthy of credibility he no longer enjoys. Great responsibility is placed upon Prosecution counsel, and although his description as a minister of justice may sound pompous to modern ears but accurately describes the way in which he should discharge his function." Your Honours, I don't think it makes any difference whether that be a statement addressed to the role of prosecuting counsel in a domestic jurisdiction of a member state of the United Nations as to what the role of prosecuting counsel before this court is. And those duties, in my respectful submission, are the duties encumbent upon all prosecutors. Your Honours, in this jurisdiction, there is a broad cross-section of national backgrounds of counsel that appear before the Tribunal. This applies both to the Prosecution and to the Defence. Matters which, in some jurisdiction, are considered taboo or contrary to ethics or etiquette of the bar might, in other jurisdictions, be completely or totally acceptable. This may range from any number of issues, including the dealing with witnesses or the presentation of evidence in the court. There are very many differences. Sometimes these differences may appear to offend because they are contrary to some etiquette or practice which one is accustomed to in their own national jurisdiction. There is one matter, Your Honour, which I think is common to all prosecutors who are generally pursuing their work. And that is that under no circumstances should ever a conviction be put before justice. And so it is with the case of the accused, Mr. Dokmanovic, Your Honours. If Your Honours are satisfied that the Prosecution has not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt, it is, as it is the duty of any Tribunal, in fact, your duty to acquit. But equally if you are satisfied that it has been so proved, it is your duty to convict. Your Honours, I now wish to touch upon a number of other issues that arise in my submission on matters of the law. And the first I would like to touch upon is the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions. And, Your Honours, in our case, in our submission, in the case that's now before you for determination, it is our submission that there is no question whatsoever on the facts that the Prosecution has proved beyond all reasonable doubt that at the relevant time and place, an armed conflict existed between two independent and sovereign states, thus rendering it international in character. Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Williamson, may elaborate on those facts which we say prove this matter beyond a reasonable doubt. But the question is, Your Honours, is it necessary for the Prosecution to prove it beyond a reasonable doubt or to prove it at all? Your Honours may be aware that this has been the subject of some discussion in academic circles in other places. And there is no question that the application of the grave breach provisions to this Tribunal and the practical application of them in the setting of a criminal court is something which is in its very early days, its very infancy. And I don't think anyone can say that there is any finally settled point of view which prevails over all others in this area. It's our respectful submission that it is appropriate to look at this question. It is appropriate to look at it, particularly in a case where the evidence clearly proves the issue beyond a reasonable doubt, so that there can be no question of injustice to any accused persons. Your Honours, with respect to the issue of whether or not it can be said that the matter needs to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, that an international armed conflict existed, I am unable to assist Your Honours with any law at all where this has been examined and determined that it must be so proved. If it is not to be so proved beyond a reasonable doubt, the question is: Does it become in the nature of a jurisdictional question? If that be so, then is it essential that it be proved beyond a reasonable doubt? There is argument, Your Honours, that when it is merely a jurisdictional question, if it's a jurisdictional issue that needs to be proved by the Prosecution, then it may, perhaps in those circumstances, in those limited circumstances, merely have to be proved on the balance of probabilities. That is one possibility. The other possibility that I postulate, Your Honours, for Your Honours' consideration is the fact that, is it necessary for the Prosecution to prove the question of the international character of the conflict beyond a reasonable doubt at all? Your Honours, international setting, and as a general rule, courts do not accept jurisdiction over offences committed outside their national boundaries. True it is that the legislature of many national courts can invest a court with extra territorial jurisdiction. But unless such jurisdiction is clearly expressed in the legislation, it is not common for courts to accept such extra territorial jurisdiction. The reason for this, Your Honours, is to be found in the committee of nations, namely, that courts do not wish to offend foreign courts by usurping their authority over what has happened in their country. It is because of this very reluctance, in our submission, that when the drafters of the 1949 Conventions wished to introduce the concept of universal jurisdiction, they had to devise a mechanism which was to be included in the conventions to overcome the automatic application by national courts of what is sometimes referred to as terminatory jurisdiction. The concept of grave breaches was born in 1949 in those conventions, and thus the 1949 Geneva Convention systems for repression of grave breaches is not based on International Tribunals, but rather on national enforcement and adjudication before national courts. Hence, when an International Tribunal looks for the basis to try grave breaches, it's not, in my respectful submission, to Common Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions that it must look, but it must look to its own statutory base, which, in the case of this Tribunal, is Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal. Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal makes no reference to Common Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions, nor would it, in my submission, because that Article is expressly designed to overcome the reticence of national courts to try offences that occur on the territory of another state. It is only when the special preconditions of Common Article 2 have been met can a national court then venture into the area of universal jurisdiction. Indeed, such is the reluctance of such national courts to apply universal jurisdiction, notwithstanding the existence of Common Article 2, but in those countries, special legislation is introduced through their government and parliament to permit the courts to expressly apply universal jurisdiction in those circumstances where the principles of Common Article 2 would be satisfied. Your Honours, nor does Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal refer to international armed conflict or the sovereignty of independent and internationally recognised states. The reason why, in my submission, that an International Tribunal such as this need not concern itself with the issues such as jurisdictional elements is because it is a product of the community of nations, it is not concerned itself with the committee of nations. Thus, when the community of nations create a body such as the Tribunal, it is to be inferred that no further jurisdictional prerequisites, such as Common Article 2, need to be complied with before such jurisdiction is exercised. That is not to say, Your Honours, that the internationality of the conflict is irrelevant. Your Honours, until the time is reached when it can be asserted with confidence that customary international law has changed the scope of the grave breach provisions to the point that the classification of the conflict is no longer a relevant issue, one must assume that the classification of the conflict for both states and international tribunals is a matter of significance. However, Your Honours, it may be that the significance of the international nature of the conflict is a matter which may concern the Defence in raising a challenge to the jurisdiction based on the lack of internationality. In other words, when confronted with an indictment which charges grave breach provisions, the approach may be for the Tribunal to embark upon the hearing on the assumption that it has jurisdiction, rightly and properly conferred, by virtue of Article 2 of its own Statute. There is a mechanism provided not only in the Rules but, it must be assumed, by the Statute itself, for the Defence to raise an issue of jurisdiction at the outset of the proceedings claiming the lack of internationality and thereby arguing that the grave breach provisions do not appropriately form part of the charges in this case because of the absence of internationality of the conflict. That then is a matter which is disposed of at the initial stages of the proceedings and is to determined, because it is raised by the Defence, on the balance of probabilities. It may be that, Your Honours, is the appropriate approach to take in such matters. If that were so, then one could imagine that the extensive evidence called in support of proof of internationality of the conflict and of the sovereignty of states to the conflict would then become unnecessary in the order of course of events. It is not customary in prosecutions for the Prosecution to commence its case at the outset by establishing in evidence that the court has jurisdiction. The usual approach is for the court to assume jurisdiction and to proceed to deal with the matter. But as I have said, the Defence can always challenge that. That, Your Honours, would be a considerable departure from the approach adopted in previous cases, but it may, in fact, be the correct approach to apply. Your Honours, I raise this against a backdrop of the fact that, in our respectful submission, the evidence clearly demonstrates beyond a reasonable doubt that an international armed conflict occurred in Vukovar on November the 20th, 1991, between the then internationally recognised Sovereign State of Croatia and the Sovereign State of Serbia, and that the conflict between the two states was engaged in by forces of the alternative and opposite sides. I make this submission against that background. Your Honours, the only other matter that I wish to touch upon, unless there are issues which I can assist you with on questions of law, was the issue of sentencing. I mentioned earlier in my closing address the question of different perceptions and different approaches taken in some national jurisdictions to various issues, and there can be a difference too with respect to the question of sentencing. In some jurisdictions, the Prosecution makes no comment on sentence. It is a matter entirely for the court. The Prosecution, once it has closed its case and once the evidence is all in for determination, the Prosecution rests and makes no further submission on this issue because that is a matter for the exclusive domain of the court. In jurisdictions where that was traditionally accepted as being the state of the law, in more recent times, in some of those jurisdictions, there has been a shift. The primary basis for the shift has been because, in those jurisdictions almost invariably, an appeal against a sentence imposed by a court, trial court, has been permitted by the legislature. Appeal courts reason that it hardly behoves the Prosecution to complain about the manifestly inadequate sentence of an accused person on appeal if it sat mute during the whole process of sentencing and not expressed its view whatsoever. Your Honours, this Tribunal is in a situation where there exists an appeal against sentence, so one assumes that the Prosecution is to take the more perhaps modern approach having regard to that appeal capacity, but that the Prosecution is further reinforced in commenting on sentence having regard to the wording of Rule 100 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of this Tribunal which expressly provide for comment upon sentence to be made by the parties, including the Prosecution, in appropriate circumstances. Your Honours, I trust that my written submissions will be of some assistance to you, and I don't wish to take any further time now. I defer to my colleague, Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Since January of this year, Your Honours have heard a substantial number of witnesses. You have had the conflict in Vukovar brought to life in this courtroom. You have heard it through the voices of those unfortunate people who had to live through the battle and you have seen it through their eyes. But as much as those people suffered, this trial has been about the 200 or more persons who suffered even more and who were, in the end, brutally murdered simply because they were not Serbs. This case has not been a debate about how the war started or who started it. Those are questions for historians and, fortunately, we are not called upon to decide those issues. It is fair to say that many mistakes were made by both sides to the conflict, and that there are no shortage of people who share in the responsibility for what ultimately happened. No one will argue that in 1991, the Serbs in Croatia did not have some legitimate grievances. A nationalistic government had come to power, and Serbs saw many of the privileges that they had enjoyed in Yugoslavia slipping away. Rather than pursue dialogue, they chose armed conflict. As soon as the first feeble attempts at negotiation broke down, it was all too easy for the Serbs to embrace the government of Slobodan Milosevic which was just as nationalistic, if not more so, than the government in Zagreb. Milosevic was holding out the promise of Greater Serbia, and to Croatian Serbs, this was much more attractive than any arrangement with the Croats, no matter how much autonomy they would be given. So if the Croats wouldn't accede to all of their demands, then the Serbs would beat them into submission and force them to do so. The Croats made mistakes, as Stipe Mesic told you. They didn't try hard enough to reach a middle ground with the Serbs, but ultimately, that didn't cause this war. It only served as a pretext, an excuse, whereby those men in Belgrade and Knin and Vukovar could use military force to pursue their dream of Greater Serbia. The Serbs did not wish to reach accommodation with the Croats in 1991, for they knew that they had superior force. Why should they compromise on anything when they could force their will and get everything? They chose war not because they had to, they chose war because they were sure they would win. The people of Vukovar were among the first to pay the price for that choice, and the price they paid was more than anyone could have imagined. Croatia and Slovenia both declared independence on June 25th, 1991. The JNA quickly moved against Slovenia, but within ten days, the fighting was over, and the JNA announced its intention to quit Slovenia. At that time, the EC troika was heavily involved in a diplomatic initiative to resolve the problems surrounding the break-up of Yugoslavia. They realised already at that point that Yugoslavia was finished, but they wished to find a framework under which the dissolution could take place peacefully. One of the components of this strategy was to delay implementation of Croatia and Slovenia's declarations of independence. Thus, agreement was reached that a moratorium would be placed on the implementation of independence for 100 days or until October 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sorry. I am not receiving the Serbian interpretation, nor is the accused. I apologise, Mr. Williamson, for interrupting you, but you're not being interpreted into Serbian. That's the reason why I interrupted. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I have been going too fast, I apologise, if that is the problem, but if it's a technical problem, perhaps it's been corrected. As you heard Stipe Mesic testify, the EC countries realised that Croatia's and Slovenia's independence was a fact. It was only a question of trying to fit implementation of that into the framework of an overall solution for Yugoslavia. Thus, the delay in implementation was requested for political reasons, not because legal impediments were recognised. What took place in the 100 days that this moratorium was in effect? Croatia took the steps which allowed it to implement its full independence on the 8th of October, 1991. During these 100 days, the National Guard was transformed into the Croatian army. Croatia gave a structure to its government, and the government started functioning in a manner totally independent from the old federal Yugoslav organs in Belgrade. Croatia established border posts all along its frontiers with Slovenia and Hungary and at its coastal ports. The fact is, Yugoslavia, as a viable entity, had ceased to exist long before 8 October, 1991. Perhaps the clearest indication of this was the diminishing role of the federal presidency in international affairs. By autumn, the International Community was dealing with Slobodan Milosevic and Franjo Tudjman and the other republic presidents. They now held the power. The members of the federal presidency were relegated to the sidelines, and by the time of the last Hague conference, they were not even in attendance. A lot of things factored into the destruction of Yugoslavia: Slobodan Milosevic's desire to dominate all of Yugoslavia and the steps that he took to achieve that; dissatisfaction in Croatia and Slovenia with the financial set-up of Yugoslavia; the desire in those republics for real autonomy. All of these things contributed to the break-up, and it is hard to say what caused what. But I believe the evidence supports the notion that Slobodan Milosevic and Serbia had an important role in the demise of Yugoslavia. Certainly a role greater than any German Vatican conspiracy. This is due to the fact that the Yugoslavia that Slobodan Milosevic wanted, the Yugoslavia that Slavko Dokmanovic wanted, was, in fact, Greater Serbia. It wasn't a Yugoslavia built on the old foundations of brotherhood and unity, it was a Yugoslavia built on Serb dominance and it was a Yugoslavia that no one else could stomach. But the Serbian leadership was determined to achieve this kind of Yugoslavia, this Greater Serbia, and the JNA was the tool by which they would do it. If you seek to know the true role of the JNA, then look at the events of July 1991. After ten days of fighting, the JNA stopped fighting in Slovenia. JNA barracks were surrounded there. There was absolutely nothing different about Slovenia's secession than Croatia's. Slovenia was every bit as much a part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as was Croatia. Its departure affected the integrity of Yugoslavia just as much as the departure of Croatia. If the JNA was really fighting to maintain Yugoslavia, then why withdraw from Slovenia and let it goes its own way? The JNA's motives were made clear the minute they started pulling out of Slovenia. It is a point they cannot reconcile, because from that juncture on, it is impossible for them to say that this was a fight to maintain Yugoslavia. It had become a fight for Serbia and the Serbs. As the summer of 1991 progressed, the transformation of the JNA continued as the army became more and more Serbian. An officer core that was already heavily dominated by Serbs and Montenegrins was now coupled with a force of soldiers who were primarily Serb and Montenegrin. The old ideas of an army that mirrored the population of all of Yugoslavia were gone. The Slovenes had left, the Croats had left; Bosnians and Macedonians were not reporting for duty. There were huge shortages in manpower, and these were filled only by mobilising Serb Territorial Defence units and enlisting the help of Serb paramilitary groups like Arkan's and Seselj's. Every time a non-Serb left, a Serb replaced them. The JNA had become the army of Serbia, and the power behind the army had shifted away from the federal Yugoslav bodies to the Serbian president, Slobodan Milosevic. The ultimatum of 1 October, 1991, from the general staff of the JNA to the president of Croatia, the government of Croatia, and the general staff of the Croatian army, makes clear who was at war. On one side, there is Croatia and its army; and on the other side, there is the JNA fighting alongside its Serb allies. The war had become a fight between Serbia and Croatia. As this was happening, the Croatian community in Eastern Slavonia became more and more isolated. The JNA's role changed there. It was no longer the intermediaries separating the combatants. It had clearly decided to join the side of one of the combatants, the Serbs, and in doing so it became the device for creating Greater Serbia. First, the JNA sought to "liberate" the Croatian villages in the Vukovar municipality. Interestingly enough, what the JNA termed as "liberation" translated into death, destruction, and expulsion for the Croats. The actions of the JNA were well-orchestrated. They were done with a single purpose in mind, and that was to force the Croats from the homes they had lived in for centuries and to secure those territories for Serbia. The local Serbian leadership are already decided that this area was part of Serbia. Its pronouncements and its rulings are clear evidence of this effect. The Serbs had effectively cut themselves out of Croatia and made the region a part of Serbia. All that remained to be done was to defeat the Croats in the region and to get them out of the way. No one can argue that the JNA and their local Serb allies were anything but effective in this endeavour. The Croat villages of Sotin, Sarengrad, Lovas, Bapska and Tovarnik were attacked. Their citizens were killed or tortured or terrorised into leaving their homes. One by one, as these villages emptied, their residents came to the only place they could go, Ilok, and in the first large scale ethnic cleansing of the war, the JNA surrounded that helpless, isolated town, and began stepping up the threats. Their kind neighbours in Backa Palanka, across the river in Serbia, did their part by cutting off the electricity and the yeast supplies to Ilok. When it became obvious to the people there that they had either to suffer the same fate as the other Croatian villages or to go, the JNA gladly provided buses to take them away. If you doubt for one second the intent of the JNA in all of this, read again the ultimatum to the people of Bapska, where they were told if they did not comply with the army's demands, "their village will cease to exist on a geographical map." Listen again to the words of General Andrija Biorcevic, the JNA's operational commander for the Vukovar military theatre. When talking of his Serb paramilitary allies, he says, "We surround a village, they enter it, kill those who refuse to surrender, and we go on." This was no longer the army of Yugoslavia. The JNA and their Serb paramilitary allies were engaged in a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population. It is evidenced by those who survived it, by the 21 men marched to their death in a mine field in Lovas, by the occupation of Baranja, by the 1300 bodies pulled out of the mass grave in Vukovar, and by the overall JNA commander in the region who boasts about it. After Ilok, the sole outpost for Croats in Eastern Slavonia was Vukovar. It stood alone, ringed by hundreds of artillery pieces, tanks, gun boats on the Danube, and some 30.000 troops. Inside the siege line, about 10.000 civilians and a little less than 2.000 defenders held out. They lived in cellars for three months while thousands upon thousands of shells were lobbed onto their dying city, but they continued to hold out. You have heard what the people of Vukovar went through as the noose tightened around their city. By mid November, the battle was clearly lost. They could only await their so-called "liberation." Knowing what would come, they sought any way they could find to safeguard themselves against the murder which would follow. The world too had already seen enough of the new JNA to realise that this once proud and dignified fighting force had been reduced to something entirely different. But despite everything the JNA had already done, the world community still thought that the army would abide by its own agreements, that the commitments of its generals meant something. It was still early enough, though, that people were shocked when the images of Major Sljivancanin were broadcast around the world as he blocked the ICRC and the ECMM from reaching Vukovar hospital. There can be no doubt as to what happened to the men taken from Vukovar hospital on the morning of the 20th of November, 1991. The few survivors attest to it, the grieving families left behind attest to it, but most of all, the 200 bodies pulled out of the ground at Ovcara attest to it. Why were these 198 men and two women killed at Ovcara? Ultimately, they were killed for one reason and one reason alone: That being the fact that they were not Serbs. There was no longer room for anyone other than Serbs in Vukovar except perhaps for a few elderly Croats or those that were married to Serbs. Slavko Dokmanovic certainly makes it clear in the two interviews we have heard from that period when he says "Vukovar is a Serbian city." The decision to make Vukovar a Serbian city was accomplished at its most horrific with the killings at Ovcara. The Serb authorities in Vukovar and the Republic of Serb Krajina did not want the world to see what they had done. They did not want the world to see the criminal foundations upon which they had built their state. They did not want the world to see that they had turned Sinisa Veber from a strong young athlete into a rotting corpse. They did not want the world to see that they had turned 16-year-old Igor Kacic from a scared kid holding onto a stuffed mouse into a rotting corpse. But they had. They had turned at least 200 living, breathing persons with families, with friends, they had turned them into a jumble of dead bodies decomposing in an isolated grave. Of course they did not want the world to see what they had done. There can be no dispute as to what ultimately happened to the victims, and there is little dispute as to the circumstances under which it occurred. The dispute here lies in terms of who was responsible for these cowardly crimes. We have seen the role of the JNA in what happened, but Sljivancanin, Mrksic, and Radic, are not on trial here today. They hide in Serbia. We have seen the role of paramilitary commanders like Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic, but they are also not on trial here today. What of the men who is on trial here now? What of Slavko Dokmanovic? Your Honour, might I ask what the schedule is anticipated being? Because I saw the note, I assume there is a request for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt you because I thought it was not very polite on my side, but actually, because of the interpreters, we should take a break. How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think I'm about a third of the way through it, so I would assume probably another 30 to 45 minutes at the most. But this is a good breaking point, if you would like to recess here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Fila, how much time do you think you need for your closing statement so that we can do some planning?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I will speak only about the case, I won't need too much time. But if I will have to deal with the other situations, like what Milosevic is like, what Tudjman is like, what the JNA did, I'll need a lot more time. So should I try talking about what the US are like, why they did not extradite their citizens, et cetera? Let us stick to the case. This way you bring me into an embarrassing situation to discuss Milosevic and Tudjman, and believe me, I am not interested in either one of them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The court too --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have the judgement of the court in the United States of America, and they did not extradite a person to the Netherlands. That is a final judgement. And I have it too. Am I supposed to talk about the United States of America, what kind of a country that is, what Mr. Williamson's president is like, and what kind of a country it is because they did not extradite this citizen? That is my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course not. We should confine ourselves to the case and to the facts that are relevant to our case, so I'm sure that you will not deal with all these other matters, Milosevic, these are of no importance whatsoever. These are absolutely immaterial to what we are discussing here. And I'm sure that Mr. Williamson as well will try to confine himself to the facts of the case. Actually, you had already started dealing only with Dokmanovic, and we are interested only in whether or not the charges against the accused are well-founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just say this, though? We are certainly not trying to wander off into matters that are irrelevant to the court and this is not meant as any kind of insult to Serbia or to Mr. Fila, but the fact is, we have to deal with issues of international armed conflict, the nature of the conflict, whether there was a widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population. Those are absolutely relevant issues to this trial. And to that extent, I have tried to point out facts that we felt establish that, and we are prepared to move on beyond that, but I take exception to Mr. Fila's comment that we have been just doing this in some effort to dirty Serbia or to downgrade him in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course not. But let me insist on one point. The court will not pay any attention to the general historical facts. We are only dealing with a case, and of course we will not dwell on the historical background which is not of special relevance to the legal and factual problems which we are discussing --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you looked at my written statement, did you find a word about Franjo Tudjman or about Croatia? I didn't say a word about that. Only about what is at stake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I wonder whether you need a lot -- much time? Could you approximately tell us how much time you need for your closing statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Certainly less than one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Because of the previous commitments of some Judges, we will now adjourn for 20 minutes, and we can go on until quarter to or ten to one, then we will have to reconvene at 2.30, if this is agreeable to you, Mr. Fila, so I imagine, Mr. Fila, you will make your closing statement at 2.30. All right? Good. Thank you. So we adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, let's look at the transformation of Slavko Dokmanovic. He was an individual who, by many accounts, was regarded as a decent man before the war. He had a family that loved him and he had a number of friends. He took great pride in the fact that many Croats had voted for him in 1990, and without them, he wouldn't have been elected. That is what makes his later actions all the more sinister. His friends all say that he was a moderate, a peacemaker. But how moderate was Slavko Dokmanovic? If he was such a moderate, such a man of peace and reconciliation, why is he not seen that way by the Croats? It seems that if he was really reaching out to them and offering a message of tolerance and reconciliation, that they, of all people, would know it. Has there been a single witness, though, who wasn't a Serb to say that he was a moderate? No. Non-Serbs and the members of the international community all saw him as an extremist. Was this all a big misunderstanding, or did Slavko Dokmanovic, when times were different, say things and do things which led people to believe that he was an extremist, a radical Serb who hated Croats and who pursued the goal of Greater Serbia? There were plenty of people on both sides of Vukovar who held extremist views, but relatively few of them were in positions where these views had a real affect on other people. Slavko Dokmanovic was among those relative few because no one can doubt his political prominence. He was the president of the municipal assembly from 1990 onwards. We have seen the legislation of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. We have seen the pronouncements of the Serbian National Council. They have written that Croatian law does not apply and that the Croatian government has no authority. These people were in armed revolt against Croatian authority. They did not recognise anything that the Croatian government was telling them to do, yet the decision of the Croatian government removing Dokmanovic from office is held up as proof that he was no longer in power. Admittedly, in the ever diminishing areas under Croatian control, Slavko Dokmanovic wasn't the mayor. But among the Serbs who were trying to rest those arrests from Croat control, he was still the rightful mayor. Because Queen Wilhelmina was forced into exile during the German occupation of World War II, it didn't change the views of the Dutch that she was their rightful queen. To the Serbs of Vukovar municipality, Croatian control of the city of Vukovar was also viewed as an illegal occupation, thus the need to liberate it. We can only speculate on what power Slavko Dokmanovic exercised among Serbs as their rightful mayor during this period for we really don't know. There was a state of war developing, so things weren't functioning in the same way as they would have in peace time. The legislation regulations which govern the functioning of municipal government in Vukovar, however, made provision for the mayor to continue exercising power during wartime or state of emergency. To what extent this was done, we can't say. Yet we can say from the evidence that Slavko Dokmanovic still carried on with his political role the best that he could. In August 1991, when the government of the Serbian district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was formed, Slavko Dokmanovic became a minister, again, a term he refused to use when asked point-blank by Mr. Milner in his interview if that was his job, again, a term that all his counterparts used to describe themselves, and a term which is set out in the legislation of the Serbian district. Within this government, Slavko Dokmanovic had the portfolio for agriculture, and great efforts have been made to portray him as the simple agronomist. This government, though, was the executive authority for the whole region under Serbian control. It had links with the local Serb forces, the Territorial Defence, and the paramilitaries, which they now seek to downplay. This government, which allegedly has no military roles, is full of ministers and a prime minister who wear military uniforms. It is receiving reports from military commanders. It is resolving problems between the Territorial Defence and the JNA. It is providing supplies to the military. It is issuing pronouncements on the relationship between itself and the army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could Mr. Williamson slow down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It has, according to Milan Knezevic, an agreement with the JNA that members of the government will not be in the army. What greater recognition could you have by the JNA of the primacy of the government? By exempting these people from military service, when everyone else is obligated to fight, it shows that the JNA felt that the government had a role of importance which had to be carried out, and even military service in wartime had to be subordinated to it. What of all these stories that the Defence puts forward that Slavko Dokmanovic had no power or influence because he was viewed as a bad Serb, a man despised in his own community. I am sure that among some Serbs, he wasn't well-liked, such as the nature of political office. People who hold public office cannot please everyone all the time, but I would suggest to the court that these stories have been greatly exaggerated, once again in an attempt to adapt to what is acceptable now that times are different. Let's look at the government of which Slavko Dokmanovic was a part, the government of the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, the government of Goran Hadzic. What did this government stand for? What did it represent? It was a government built on the misery and suffering of anyone who wasn't a Serb. It was a government that used ethnic cleansing to secure territory over which it could rule. It was a government that hungered for even more territory after it had gotten a totally destroyed Vukovar. After the horrible cost of war there, the thousands of persons killed, the city in ruins, Goran Hadzic jubilantly says they should move toward the Serbian border, should expand further. I will submit to you that one of the few truthful things that Goran Hadzic said in his testimony to this court was that things were not normal then. He is absolutely right about that. At least in the eyes of the Vukovar Serbs, things were very different in 1991. In 1991, they had won. Serbia had proved it was right because it had crushed the Croats. All of their rhetoric of hate and murder was perfectly acceptable. It was the foundation of their power, and safely situated behind their razor wire and mine fields, they were part of Mother Serbia. Nobody could touch them. They could do anything they wanted to the Croats. They could literally get away with murder. They could not imagine that one day the land from which they expelled all of the Croats would again become a real part of Croatia. They could not imagine that one day someone would dig up the mass graves, that one day a court would be established to hold persons responsible for war crimes, but all of these things have happened. Times have, indeed, changed. And the convoluted and inconsistent explanations that you hear in court now for what they said and did then are the strong confirmation there is for the fact that times are different now. Actions and words for which they had no shame in 1991 now must be explained away for they have come back to haunt them. What was the role of this government of Goran Hadzic and Slavko Dokmanovic on the 20th of November, 1991? We know that there was a meeting in Erdut on the 19th. We have the minutes from that meeting, and we know, to some extent, what was discussed there, but a lot of mystery surrounds the meeting of the 20th in Vukovar. We have heard varying reasons for why this meeting took place, many of which are inconsistent. I will submit to Your Honours that from the early morning of 20 November, 1991, the JNA intended that the men taken from the hospital were to die. The behaviour of the JNA officers and the statements that they make, particularly Major Sljivancanin, corroborate this. But when the prisoners were taken to the JNA barracks, I would suggest to you that the JNA did not want to take this action alone. It wanted a civilian authority to give its blessing to the killings. As do most armies in the world, the JNA also desired official sanction from civilian authorities for its actions. Look at the testimony of Stipe Mesic as to what went on in the federal presidency from January through October 1991 as the JNA repeatedly sought the presidency's blessings for its operations. Thus, while the buses waited at the JNA barracks, Major Sljivancanin crossed over the road to VELEPROMET to get the blessing of the Serbian District Government, to get the seal of legitimacy for the crimes which were about to be committed. There is no way that we can know exactly what was said at VELEPROMET or how it was decided that these men and women were to be killed at Ovcara. Short of one of the participants coming into court and saying that they took a decision to kill 200 people, I'll submit to you that such an occurrence is extremely unlikely. Anyone who took part in that decision is a principal to this crime, and few people are willing to admit to involvement in such an act. The evidence is very compelling, however, that such a decision was taken at VELEPROMET. Look at all of the circumstances that surround this meeting and look at what follows it. I'd like to draw a parallel from history, if I may, and in doing so, I'm not, in any way, attempting to equate the crimes but, rather, point out the manner in which crimes are planned. Consider the Wansee Conference which took place outside Berlin in 1942. It's generally agreed that this was the meeting at which the decision was taken to exterminate the Jewish population in Europe, what was referred to as the final solution. The only hard evidence coming out of that meeting was a memorandum which talks about transport of Jews and says that utilisation of Jewish labour was crucial, that those who couldn't work would be treated accordingly. By itself, the document means little, but when it is examined in the context of what we know happened to Jews in Europe, the import of that meeting is made clear. When meetings of this sort are held, meetings to plan crimes, it is very unusual that persons outside the group involved actually knows what transpired. Any group of criminal conspirators is going to try to keep their conspiracy secret. It is the nature of conspiratorial acts. Rarely a conspiracy is revealed when one of the conspirators breaks the silence and tells someone outside the group. More often than not, though, evidence of conspiracies comes in the form of overt acts which take place afterward and which tend to show a course of action which was agreed upon by the conspirators. Such is the case here. Look at the minutes from the meeting of November 19th in Erdut which say that the JNA will come under the control of the government. Then a meeting takes place on the 20th of which no records are kept. Look at the presence of Arkan and Sljivancanin. Look at the fact that the buses are held at the JNA barracks for at least two hours. It is clear that word has gotten around about what is happening. Surely this hasn't escaped the attention of the government meeting across the road, and surely Major Sljivancanin, who had gone to such lengths to conceal his crimes from the international monitors, is not going to just abandon the process while these prisoners are situated at the main JNA in the area. Sljivancanin goes to VELEPROMET for a reason. The government meets there for a reason, and then the buses suddenly have a destination and move out. What were they waiting on? Why were they held there for two or more hours? Why does Goran Hadzic leave and return several times? We can't answer these questions precisely because we weren't there, and no one who was there is going to make us privy to exactly what transpired. So we have to look at the overt acts which take place contemporaneous to and in the aftermath of the government meeting. We have to look to the words of Goran Hadzic spoken that very evening from Sid when he says that the government's "main resolution was that the detained Ustashas whom we have captured would not leave the territory of the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem." He says that they have reached agreement with the military authorities as to this. Are these all just coincidences? Isn't it more logical to take Goran Hadzic's words and attribute to them the obvious meaning? Doesn't it make more sense, looking at everything that happened, to conclude that what he said in 1991 was the truth and that the 1998 version is one constructed for this court now that the crime has been exposed and one of his ministers is in gaol. If these are coincidences, then why did Slavko Dokmanovic not want to mention the government meeting at VELEPROMET? Look at his interview on the aeroplane. Look at the interview he gave in the prison. Look at all of the opportunities he has to say something about this meeting. Look at the direct questions put to him by Mr. Milner in this regard. Why the evasion on his part? Even after he mentions going to VELEPROMET, he steadfastly avoids discussion of this meeting. What happened there that makes him so reluctant to associate himself with it? The Defence has made great efforts to characterise it as something other than what it was. Isn't it more logical, though, and likely that all of these things that happened were not coincidence? Rather, the explanation for these things is the obvious one, that persons in the government took the decision that Goran Hadzic said they did, and that was, in fact, carried out with the execution of 200 or more men and went at Ovcara hours after he announced the decision on Belgrade television. After this fateful meeting at VELEPROMET concludes, what does Slavko Dokmanovic do? He goes to the centre of Vukovar. He and his companions drive around. Everything they see they blame on the Croats. When they see a building destroyed, they automatically assume it must have been destroyed by the Croats. When they see dead bodies, they automatically assume they must be Serbs killed by Croats. Today the witnesses say they weren't angry and that they didn't blame the Croats. But if you have any doubts, listen to the tape, listen to them curse the Croats and their Ustasha mothers at everything they see. I will submit to you that after leaving the centre of Vukovar, Slavko Dokmanovic decides to go to Ovcara himself. He was at VELEPROMET. He knows what is going to happen to these men, that they are all going to be killed. He just can't resist going out there and seeing it for himself. You can imagine the reason Slavko Dokmanovic went there, the once proud mayor of Vukovar, chased from his rightful office by the Croats, the bitterness of those months of exile in Trpinja, still recognised as mayor by the Serbs, but without access to his seat of government because it is occupied by the Ustashas. You can imagine the hate, the frustration, and the anger. Then the anger of all those months compounded by what he sees in Vukovar, the bodies, the destroyed Serbian church, all done by the Croats. You hear his interview that Vukovar will be forever Serbian; there is no room for Croats. If you seek the reason why Slavko Dokmanovic needed to go to Ovcara, look at the reason why every other Serb went there? Look at why these captive men and women were held at the hangar for several hours. It would have been easy enough just to kill them straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But it wasn't enough to do that, to murder unarmed, defenceless prisoners in cold blood. What Ovcara was about was punishment. The Serbs had won. The Croats were vanquished. They had to be beaten and terrorised and tortured so that they would know that when they went to their death that the Serbs had been right and they had been wrong. The Serbs wanted to rub it in their faces that they had lost. The victors couldn't resist pouring salt in the wounds of their helpless victims. But times are different then, and no Serb who was at Ovcara ever expected that a Croat who was there would have the opportunity to sit in a witness box and point the finger at him for having taken part, but it has happened. You have heard men who survived that brutal day come in this courtroom and point their fingers at Slavko Dokmanovic and say, "You were there." You have heard him say how the accused, when he recognised him, Cakalic said, "So you too are here, Inspector." He couldn't resist being a part of that. He too needed his pound of fresh. He needed to repay the humiliation he felt at being stopped by the Croatian police, he, the elected mayor of Vukovar. He needed to show the other Serbs there that he was just as radical as they were. There was no longer any need to sit on the fence. The victory of the Serbs was overwhelming and clear cut. The victory was based on ethnic hatred and intolerance. The government in which Dokmanovic served had its foundation on those bases. How better to show that he was one of them, one who embraced hatred and violence every bit as the most radical of Serbs. How better to silence Serb critics who said he wasn't extremist enough. This was easy, after all. He knew these men were to be killed. How did Slavko Dokmanovic know that these men were going to be killed? He knew it because he had been at VELEPROMET where the decision was taken. Even outside the confines of the government meeting, it was common knowledge at VELEPROMET as to what was going to happen. The buses are parked just down the street. Everyone is talking about it. Witness DB certainly knows about it. This is a man who is in Dokmanovic's company that day. He is all over the videotape. He goes over to the barracks to have a look. He tells Cakalic that he's on the wrong bus and then goes on to say that all of the buses are the same. He knows the fate of these men, as does everyone there. Word has spread quickly. Witness Q hears of it in another part of town. Everyone knows that the Ustashas are to be killed. One of the men who will be beaten to death at Ovcara, Damjon Samardzic, is told at the barracks that he will die. It is clear that people know what is to happen by the fact that even before the buses leave the JNA barracks, attempts are already being made to save people. After the buses arrive at Ovcara, attempts to save a lucky few continue. Slavko Dokmanovic goes to Ovcara with full knowledge of what is to transpire. What does transpire at Ovcara when he arrives? He gets there as the slow process of unloading prisoners is finally coming to an end. Six buses full of men have had to pull up in front of the hangar in turn, and prisoners have been forced off one by one. A prisoner is forced to run through the guantlet formed by JNA and local Serbs, beaten with fists, clubs, axe handles, and kicked by boots. And then another prisoner is taken off the bus to experience the same treatment, and on and on the process has gone all afternoon. Inside the hangar, the prisoners find no relief because the beatings continue there as well. Some are beaten even more brutally during this period, and we know that two men are actually beaten to death. All of this is a precursor to the executions which will take place later that evening. What about Slavko Dokmanovic makes his role at Ovcara so significant? The best answer to this question came from Emil Cakalic when he testified. Perhaps you can remember the emotion with which he said it: "I would have been happy today not to have seen him there, because I was thinking how can an intellectual, a person with whom I'd often talked in his office, who knew these people, I was asking myself, how could he do that?" Despite all the attempts by the Defence to portray him otherwise, the fact is that Slavko Dokmanovic was a man of influence, a man of power. He had been mayor of Vukovar. In the eyes of the Serbs, he still was. He was part of the regional government, a minister. He would be mayor again. By virtue of his political positions, he was in the highest echelons of civilian authority in the region. By virtue of his membership in the government of the Serbian District, he was in the body which coordinated the Territorial Defence and which was now assuming control of the JNA forces in the region, the same body that eight days later would reward Miroljub Vujovic, a commander at Ovcara, with appointment to the executive council running the city of Vukovar. By his presence, and even more so by his participation at Ovcara, Slavko Dokmanovic gave a blessing to the sadistic outpouring of violence. Ultimately, Your Honours, in deciding this case, it comes down to who you believe. On one hand, you have Emil Cakalic and Dragutin Berghofer. On the other hand, you have Slavko Dokmanovic and his associates who were with him at various times on the 20th of November. Let's look first at Slavko Dokmanovic and his associates. It is obvious what Mr. Dokmanovic's motivation is for lying. He wants to avoid conviction and a prison sentence. What about his colleagues? Of all of these people that we heard from who were allegedly with Mr. Dokmanovic on the 20th, relatively few were with him at the crucial period when he ventured off to Ovcara. The majority of witnesses, Witness DB, Witness DC, Vojin Susa, Boris Ivaskovic, Viselav Maletic, Ilija Koncarevic, Milos Vojnovic, Goran Hadzic, Radoslav Zlatic, Milivojevic, and Dusan Niculovic separated from Dokmanovic after the meeting in VELEPROMET or even earlier, although some say they see him a couple of hours later at Orolik. These witnesses do not provide an alibi. So that leaves Zoran Jevtovic, Jovan Cvetkovic, Vukosav Tomasevic, Nebosja Lazarevic, and Mirko Dragisic, five men. There are a number of reasons for them not to be truthful. Perhaps some or all of them accompanied Mr. Dokmanovic to Ovcara. He and Rade Leskovac, who didn't testify, were the locals. It is natural if Dokmanovic and Leskovac wished to go there that the others would follow. It was, after all, one of the sights to see in Vukovar that day. Who wouldn't want a chance to see all the Ustasha terrorists captured at last, to see the people who they felt responsible for all the death and destruction. Who wouldn't want to see the monsters capable of such crimes in Serb captivity? It wasn't far out of the way, so why not make the turn and have a look? If they went along, it makes it very clear why they too would wish to conceal the truth about what really happened. Perhaps they lied because they wanted to protect a friend or perhaps they did it, some sort of misguided belief that it helped the Serb cause. Maybe it was for all these reasons combined. We don't know. The bottom line is this, though: For whatever reason, we know that they have lied. Zoran Jevtovic, Jovan Cvetkovic, Vukosav Tomasevic, Nebosja Lazarevic, Mirko Dragisic, and the accused himself, Slavko Dokmanovic, each and all lied as to where they went. All of them testify that from the time they left the centre of Vukovar, there were no stops, turns, or changes in direction until they stopped for the buses. We know now that to be impossible, unless the videotape was altered. They all said that they stopped for the buses in Negoslavci. We now know that to be false. Even Radoslav Zlatic, the driver of Vojin Susa, was brought into this cover-up. For when he was shown the brief 21-second clip of the video from 15.42, he says with great assurance that it's Negoslavci. Look at the tape, and tell me if seeing something like that with what is shown that you could readily identify what it is. You have heard the testimony of Mr. Dzuro and Mr. Tabbush as to the efforts which were required to identify the precise spot where this was filmed. Mr. Zlatic's testimony in this regard is not credible and it is not credible because it was staged. Again, what is the significance of being where they were at 15.42 rather than Negoslavci? The spot, in and of itself, has no significance. As far as we know, no crime was committed there. They merely stopped and filmed some buses, buses which they had allegedly came up from behind but inexplicably got in front of to film, a seemingly innocent act. So why the need to lie about it? The need to lie had nothing to do with concealing the fact that they were at that spot, because that spot had no significance. So obviously there was another reason for lying. Something else had to be concealed, so it was necessary to make this spot into something that it wasn't. To accomplish this, they all had to say it was Negoslavci. It is very clear why they said this, because if they were in Negoslavci when this was filmed, it would have already put them past the turnoff to Ovcara. It would have put Mr. Dokmanovic there with them, since they testified that it was his voice. It was done to create an alibi at the point where Mr. Dokmanovic really needed it, at the point where he and his associates leave Vukovar and are getting in close proximity to Ovcara. It wouldn't have been conclusive, by any means, but it would have bolstered his story. But they got caught. They all lied about where they went. An alibi is a defence which establishes that someone could not have committed a crime because that person was somewhere else. In the absence of independent evidence, an alibi is based solely on the credibility of witnesses. In this instance, every one of those witnesses who provides an alibi for Mr. Dokmanovic, and Mr. Dokmanovic himself has been proven to have lied, I would submit to you that if they lied about this crucial point, this most crucial of points, then they did so for a reason, and it is appropriate to disregard everything in their testimony. They cannot be substantiated independently. Let's look, on the other hand, at Berghofer and Cakalic. What possible reason do they have for lying? They escaped death by the narrowest of margins. Everyone around them is brutally murdered. They too are beaten unmercifully. Why would they possibly want to blame someone for this who wasn't there instead of real perpetrators? If they were intent on nailing some Serbs for this, then why Dokmanovic? Why pick on poor Slavko? Why single him out? If this was about getting bad Serbs, then why not identify Goran Hadzic? Why not Seselj? Why not Arkan? Berghofer and Cakalic were from Vukovar. Surely they knew who many of the extremist Serbs were. Why didn't they name all of these people as being there? Why choose Dokmanovic? By everyone's account, there was no bad blood between them, no prior disagreements, no fights. Your Honours, it is clear that the Defence witnesses have reason to lie and it is obvious that they have lied. Emil Cakalic and Dragutin Berghofer have absolutely nothing to gain by identifying someone as being at Ovcara who wasn't there. They have identified Slavko Dokmanovic for one reason and one reason alone and that is because he was there. They did this of their own accord in separate interviews years ago. They identified Slavko Dokmanovic at a time when the Prosecutor had not even heard of him. If this was some great conspiracy to get Slavko Dokmanovic, why not do it right and get everyone who is rumoured to have blood on his hands? The reason is that there was no big conspiracy. There was no manufactured story. There is only the truth. And the sad truth is that Slavko Dokmanovic, a family man, a man with good friends, a man with an education, a man who was elected mayor, chose to follow the path of hatred and violence, rather than that of tolerance and compassion. It is amazing, when you listen to the Defence case, you almost get the impression that the 200 people killed at Ovcara were Serbs, that the 1300 people pulled out of the latest mass grave in Vukovar were Serbs, that all of those destroyed houses in Vukovar were those of Serbs, that the men marched into the mine field in Lovas were Serbs, that those bused out of Ilok and Vukovar were Serbs. One gets these impressions because all one hears from the Defence witnesses is how much Serbs were the victims and how Croats were to blame. But somebody killed all these people, somebody destroyed all of these houses, somebody forced all of these thousands of people out of their homes. It wasn't some mysterious force from another planet, it was their neighbours that did it, it was the army that did it, and it was the government of Goran Hadzic and Slavko Dokmanovic that did it. All of these terrible things happened, and they happened to the Croats in Vukovar; and no matter how much Slavko Dokmanovic tries to rationalise it, it was wrong. The Defence case you have heard is one of revisionist history, one which has tried to erase the ugly side of Slavko Dokmanovic, the side which is not acceptable outside the hate-filled world of Serb Vukovar of that time. It is one in which everything that was said and done in 1991 has to be cleaned up because the hate and violence are now exposed to the light of day and to people who don't agree that it was acceptable because things were different then. It is now 1998, and they tell you that what they said in television interviews and in the minutes of government meetings and in the laws that they passed isn't what it appears. They tell you that the obvious and logical meaning of those words isn't right, but that for some farfetched reason, it was necessary to say that or to express it that way. Yet, we know what happened, and we know that the things they said all came to pass. The documents and the videotaped interviews and the laws match with what we know happened, not the sanitised versions which are being offered now that things are different. What doesn't match are the stories the Defence puts forward: Don't call Slavko Dokmanovic the mayor, he was president. Don't call him a Minister, he was only an expert on agriculture. There was no meeting at VELEPROMET, only an informal gathering. He wasn't angry at the Croats, only upset. He was never an extremist, just a peacemaker and a moderate. He never visited prison camps in Serbia in uniform, he was a simple civilian. But the facts remain, the dead bodies remain, the grieving families remain, and all of the revisionist history that the Defence puts forward cannot change that. The razor wire and the mine fields no longer protect him from the outside world. It is time for Slavko Dokmanovic to now answer for what he has done.

utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I start with my closing argument, I have an obligation to fulfil towards you. I will remind you that you, Your Honours, were not very happy with me when Madam McDonald was the presiding judge. I said that this trial was not expeditious, and I said that if this trial were expeditious, I would apologise for this remark of mine. That's what I'm doing now. Now I would like to address the court and my learned colleagues from the Prosecution. First of all, I would like to say something with regard to the remark of Mr. Niemann, my learned colleague, relating to the existence of the international conflict. I could not say that what Mr. Niemann proposed was not interesting, that this should be discussed as a preliminary matter, and I think that this should find its place in an amended version of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence so that this be treated as a pre-trial matter, whether something is an international conflict or not. What I couldn't agree is that the burden of proof should be on the Defence since, in all jurisdictions, the burden of proof is always on the Prosecution. But we could deal with this much more expeditiously if we were to follow the procedure proposed by Mr. Niemann. I think he is entirely right. Before I start, one more remark. I will not be using long words or, rather, heavy words, such as "lies," that witnesses are lying. I think that these words are not at the level of this Tribunal. I also state that the Defence has never claimed that Serbs were killed at Ovcara, that Serbian houses were razed to the ground in Vukovar, that 1.200 bodies exhumed now are Serbs, I never claimed that in Pakracka Poljana that are Serbs who are buried there, although there are, and not Croats. I never claimed that the war crimes prosecuted by this Tribunal were committed by Serbs, Croats, or Muslims. The Geneva Conventions, on the basis of which this Tribunal was established, in my personal view and I think in the view of any honest men, they speak about crimes committed by non-human beings against human beings, about inhuman acts, not against Croats or Serbs or Serbs against Croats. There is not such a thing as a bad people, bad nation; there are bad individuals. I never claimed, when My Lai trials were going on, that Americans killed Vietnamese people; it was Lieutenant Kelly. We never used this judgement as evidence that somebody should be placed under house arrest for two years for killing 300 people. I will never say that Americans committed war crimes. Those who committed war crimes regardless of -- somebody killed those people. So nobody can put it to me or blame me of reviving history. I simply don't want to differentiate between people. You remember that I always offered my condolences to the victims in Vukovar. I never wanted to justify those people who did that, no matter who they are. It's not Ustashas, it's not soldiers, it's people, and people should be treated humanely. So much for the terms that we used here. Now I would like to address some legal issues. The Defence has presented its opinion in written form, and I will just provide some further explanations as to why I have those views. Article 1 of the Statute of this Tribunal is the basis for all that we are discussing here. Here we are talking about serious violations, I repeat, serious violations of international humanitarian law. Since we are looking for individual responsibility, the Prosecution prosecutes, and the Tribunal tries people who are responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law. It is the view of the Defence that this cannot apply to the case of Slavko Dokmanovic. Regardless of the reasons that have led to two Prosecutors who spoke here who have not determined exactly the time when Dokmanovic allegedly was at Ovcara, nor the time he spent there, nor the uniform that he wore at the time, nor what he actually did there, I can only conclude that they accepted the testimony of Witness Cakalic, that he was there two to five minutes. So what this Honourable Tribunal will be deciding on, it took two minutes. If I remember, for the bombing of Hiroshima, in the name of introducing democracy to Japan, it took longer than two minutes. We have four relevant places for this incident: the hospital, the barracks, the hangar at Ovcara, and the place where the people were killed. In three of those four places, the hospital, JNA barracks, and the execution site itself, the Prosecution admits that Dokmanovic was not present there. For the fourth relevant place, the hangar at Ovcara, they claim that he was there for a brief period of time, two to five minutes. Heavy words we use such as "lies" "untruths" and so on, I will not be using any words of that nature. But let me give you a historical overview of the claims made by the Prosecution about what Dokmanovic did from the time of the first indictment, on the basis of which the prima facie case was established and Judge Riad put his signature on it, I will not say that this was done in bad faith by the Prosecution, but I will point to you the difference between the indictment on the basis of which Dokmanovic was arrested and what the Prosecution said now, and they are not friends of Mr. Dokmanovic which would lead them to lie. They are not members of the government of the Serbian district. They have to speak the truth. They are bound to speak the truth, and that's what Mr. Niemann said, that in the Anglo-Saxon jurisdictions, it is the obligation of the Prosecution to speak the truth. So what did the Prosecution say when, pursuant to Rule 61, they presented the indictment against the three officers? Compared to what they have been saying now, what did the Prosecutors say when the decision was made to kill those people, they say, in hospital? Pursuant to Article 61, Sljivancanin said, "They will be eaten up by darkness," and that's what he said in the morning, and the decision of the government took place at 2.00. According to Mr. Williamson, according to what he says now, this is when the decision was made to kill them all. If you were to try those officers one day, will we be hearing the new version then? Because during the 61 proceedings, there were three important things: First, what Sljivancanin said; second, that General Mrkic was present at the hangar in Ovcara; and third, that a unit of the JNA with excavators was present there several days ago and that the victims heard those. What did we hear here at the trial against Dokmanovic? Let me tell you very briefly, just an overview. In the first indictment, which somehow forced the warrant of arrest to be issued, it is merely an adding of Dokmanovic's name next to the names of the officers. Whether this is legal, it is up to you to decide. But after Dokmanovic's arrest, which we had to wait for such a long time, so many years to take place, the indictment was amended without any evidence being led. Why? If not for the simple reason that the first indictment was necessary to force the warrant of arrest to be issued, although the Prosecution was aware at that time that Dokmanovic was not at the hospital, not at the JNA barracks, and not at the execution site, because the indictment is immediately amended, and that is the indictment that you have before you. So from the perpetrator at the same level with the three officers becomes somebody who aided and abetted, so the Prosecution was aware of that before the beginning of the trial. From the time when this indictment was issued, the Prosecution keeps changing the role it ascribes to Dokmanovic, all in the name of what Mr. Niemann said, that it is the obligation of the Prosecution to speak the truth; and what Mr. Williamson is now saying, that he has nothing to do against Mr. Dokmanovic, that he is merely here to represent the Prosecution. So on the 26th of March, they claim that JNA and Serb paramilitary soldiers, under the command or supervision of Mrkic, Radic, Sljivancanin, and Dokmanovic, on the 2nd of December, 1997. Item 28, JNA and Serb paramilitary soldiers, aided and abetted by Slavko Dokmanovic and under the command and supervision of Mrkic, Sljivancanin, and Radic; in the pre-trial brief, 15th of December, 1997, Serbian translation, page 8: The international monitors had to be misled, buses had to be organised, suitable and willing soldiers had to be found, bulldozers had to be made available to excavate the mass grave and to close it thereafter, a site for the execution had to be found. It was vital, therefore, that there be full cooperation between the Serbian military and paramilitary forces and the Serbian civilian authorities. Page 9 of the Serbian translation: It was the accused, Slavko Dokmanovic, who helped to facilitate the last part of the operation which began at the hospital and ended in Ovcara. He not only was able to provide knowledge about the site, but he also took a leadership role in the perpetration of the crimes which occurred in the farming facilities at Ovcara. Then we get a written version of the opening statement, page 16 of the English text. The same Prosecutor, all in the name of truth, states the following: Witnesses will place Dokmanovic at key positions and will identify him within key roles in the beatings at Ovcara, in the events leading up to the mass killings, demonstrating his participation in these crimes, both direct and indirect. Page 18 of the English text: The accused is criminally liable for not preventing or stopping the beatings and killings at Ovcara while he was in a position to do so because he was able to exercise control over the people who participated in committing those beatings and killings. Furthermore, it is somebody who holds authority over those who are about to commit acts, prevents them from doing so, or punishes them if the acts have already been committed. The Prosecution will show that the accused failed to fulfil this obligation. Page 19. The Prosecution must show that the accused held the position as a superior. Second, that he had actual knowledge of the crimes that were to take place or had taken place.
